title: The words the lens has
intro: The summary named the vocabulary limit, its two repairs, and two limits that have nothing to do with vocabulary. This level takes each in turn: why the limit follows from the construction rather than from a choice, how a template is actually built and what argument says it should behave like a lens vector, what the measurements show and where they are thin, and what the oracle lens buys for the price of two fine-tuned models.

chapters.title: Where the vocabulary runs out
chapters.body:
The limit follows from the construction rather than from a choice. A [[jacobian-lens]] vector is the corpus-averaged gradient of one token's output probability with respect to the residual stream. There is therefore one vector per entry of the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], and no vector for anything else ([[j-lens-vector]]).

Computing the same gradient for a longer word is not a matter of running the recipe on more text. The quantity to be differentiated would be the probability of emitting a whole sequence of tokens. That probability is only defined once the earlier tokens of the sequence have been sampled. The paper gives this as the reason the extension is not straightforward ([[multi-token-lens-extensions]]).

A second failure mode is quieter than the first. Some abstract concepts may map onto many tokens diffusely rather than onto one token sharply. The lens then has a vector for each of those tokens and a strong reading on none of them ([[single-token-limitation]]).

The paper ties this to its own intervention failures. Where a [[lens-coordinate-swap]] fails to redirect an answer, the failures fall predominantly on items whose source concept's vector was not strongly active to begin with ([[swap-success-rate]]). One reason a vector might not be active is that the model's working representation of the concept coincides with no single-token direction.

[[fig-62]] puts numbers on the decline. Across 126 multi-hop prompts, bucketed by the intermediate's length in tokens, the J-lens places that intermediate in its top ten on 98%, 48%, 32% and 7% of items at one, two, three and four-or-more tokens. The causal column falls faster still: 45%, 5%, 8% and 0%.

The obvious repair does not work. Scoring a long word by averaging the lens scores of its constituent tokens sits at or below the first-token series in every bucket. Each bucket holds between 14 and 54 items, so the [[wilson-interval|95% Wilson intervals]] are wide, and the evidence supports the shape of the curve rather than any single point on it.

chapters.title: Building a direction out of contexts
chapters.body:
The [[template-lens]] differentiates nothing. It replaces the gradient with an average over contexts.

For a word $w$, Claude is asked for short passages, each written so that $w$ is its natural continuation, each stopping just before $w$ would appear. The instruction requires the passages to vary in topic, frame and register, and forbids them from using $w$ itself. The model is then run over those passages, and the [[residual-stream]] activation at the final position is averaged across them. That gives one mean vector $\mu_w(\ell)$ per layer.

A raw mean would be dominated by whatever every passage has in common. Two corrections follow ([[template-construction]]). The mean is centered against $\mu(\ell)$, the mean over all the other words' passages, and the result is multiplied by an inverse covariance:

$$t_w(\ell) = (\Sigma_\ell + \lambda I)^{-1}\,(\mu_w(\ell) - \mu(\ell))$$

with $\lambda$ a small ridge term. Whitening by $\Sigma_\ell$ discounts the directions along which the residual stream varies most anyway. What survives is the linear discriminant direction separating contexts where the model is about to say $w$ from contexts where it is not — the object a [[linear-probe]] would fit, obtained here in closed form.

The paper offers a reason the two constructions might land in the same place. Stein's lemma states that for Gaussian $x$ and differentiable $g$, $\mathbb{E}[\nabla g(x)] = \Sigma^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}[g(x)(x-\mu)]$. Taking $x$ as the activation and $g$ as the probability that the continuation is $w$, the left-hand side is roughly what the lens computes for a single-token $w$, and the right-hand side is the template.

The conditions do not hold. Activations are not Gaussian, and $g$ depends on more than $x$. The paper presents the lemma as motivation and not as a derivation, and records a further mismatch: J-lens gradients are taken at the final residual layer and propagated through the unembedding ([[j-lens-readout]]), while these are taken from the output token probabilities.

Templates are then used like lens vectors with the unembedding step dropped. A readout projects an activation onto the templates at the same layer, and steering and swapping proceed unchanged.

chapters.title: What the templates recover, and where they misbehave
chapters.body:
Three chosen cells open the case ([[fig-61]]). At one workspace cell of the [[blackmail-scenario]] transcript, the J-lens top entries are the fragments black and ext, and the template lens returns blackmail. On a multi-hop item whose unspoken step is photosynthesis, the template lens places the whole word near the top of its ranking while the best the J-lens manages is phot ([[internal-reasoning]]). In the third panel, swapping the Tchaikovsky template for the Beethoven template across the [[workspace-layers]] turns the answer "Russian" into "German", and the mirror swap on a Beethoven prompt flips it back; the tch and beeth vectors produce neither flip.

The population evidence is the flat line beside the falling one. Across the same four length buckets, the template lens reads out at 94% to 100% and swaps at 62% down to 43%.

A control asks what the method is worth on the J-lens's own ground. Both evaluations were re-run on the paper's original 50-item [[multihop-benchmark]], where every unspoken intermediate is a single token ([[fig-63]]). The template lens reads out 42 of 50 against the J-lens's 38, and swaps 26 of 50 against 34. The intervals overlap heavily at that sample size, and the paper reads the result as parity rather than as a win for either.

Three defects are reported. The first is inherited: like the [[tuned-lens]], the template lens fits a linear predictor of the model's output, and its readouts sometimes skip to the answer in early layers instead of surfacing the intermediate ([[layer-bands]]). The second sits at the other end. On post-training transcripts whose next sampled word is in the template vocabulary, that word reaches the top ten only 67% of the time, weaker than the J-lens is at [[next-token-prediction]]; applying the normalization layer before projecting helps and does not close the gap. The third is a small set of words that surface near the top of many transcripts with no apparent relevance. Deleting them from the vocabulary works, and the paper calls the fix unprincipled.

chapters.title: Dropping the word list
chapters.childScope: Walk the [[oracle-training]] pipeline stage by stage — the [[reconstructor-model]] and its whitened cosine loss, the 3.4-million-phrase dictionary, the matching-pursuit teacher, the supervised and RL stages, and the inference-time refit — then what [[fig-64]] shows, the [[delimiter-commentary]] split, and the contrast with a [[natural-language-autoencoder]].
chapters.body:
Enumeration is what breaks first. A template exists only for a word someone listed in advance, and listing every phrase is not possible. The per-word price compounds it: a few hundred forward passes for each template, against one set of backward passes per layer for the entire J-lens.

The [[oracle-lens]] drops the list. Given an activation, it returns a short set of free-form phrases whose template vectors, combined sparsely and non-negatively, approximately reconstruct that activation. Four stages build it, run here on Haiku 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]).

A [[reconstructor-model]] comes first: a copy of the subject model fine-tuned to map a short phrase to the activation that immediately precedes it. Pairs are drawn from Assistant-turn text by sampling a position, taking the next $N$ tokens as the phrase with $N$ uniform on one to thirty-two, and taking the residual stream at the preceding position as the target. The loss is [[cosine-similarity|cosine]] error in the template lens's whitened metric, and every later stage works in that whitened space.

The remaining three stages train a proposer ([[oracle-training]]). A dictionary of roughly 3.4 million phrase vectors is built by pushing continuations of five different lengths through the reconstructor. A teacher then decomposes a million held-out activations against that dictionary by non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit, recording up to sixteen phrases each. The oracle itself is a second fine-tuned copy trained to reproduce those lists, then refined by reinforcement learning that rewards explained variance directly.

The reported accuracy is modest and stated plainly. The refined oracle explains on average 31% of whitened activation variance on held-out on-policy transcripts.

What it surfaces is shown on nine hand-picked prompts ([[fig-64]]). At the sign-off of the blackmail email the oracle reads blackmail him by revealing and expose his affair and. At the indentation before a buggy return it reads delete keys while iterating and TypeError: dictionary changed. At most positions the phrases read as upcoming text, but at delimiters they often read as commentary on the situation instead ([[delimiter-commentary]]).

chapters.title: Two limits that are not about words
chapters.body:
Setting the vocabulary aside leaves two problems that no larger vocabulary would fix.

The first is the shape of the readout. A lens readout is a ranked set of independently active directions, which is what the [[linear-representation-hypothesis]] buys: an activation decomposes into a sum of sparsely active concept directions, and nothing in that decomposition records a relation between two of them. A readout containing spider, legs and eight reports that those three concepts are present. It says nothing about how they are bound together ([[bag-of-concepts-limitation]]).

The paper's own advice for reading a readout already concedes the point, telling a reader to treat the list as a bag of ideas ([[lens-readout-reading-heuristics]]). It then states the consequence in its own terms: it is plausible that the model composes concepts into relations, assigns them roles, or organizes them under some richer grammar, and a flat readout could not see any of that. If so, the [[j-space]] as characterized here is a useful first approximation rather than a complete one.

The second problem is that some readouts do not resolve at all. At certain positions and layers the top tokens are ones the authors cannot make sense of ([[uninterpretable-readouts]]).

Three causes are offered and none is chosen between: noise in the [[averaged-jacobian]] procedure, concepts that lack single-token names, or genuine content the authors fail to recognize. The paper states that it has not characterized this systematically. It gives no rate, so this limit is reported as the authors' experience of using the lens rather than as a measurement, and a reader applying the lens to new contexts is told to expect readouts that resist interpretation alongside the ones that do not.
